criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Several ethical issues identified (defective shipping, public safety, professional integrity) with clear stakeholder enumeration and organisational context. Depth of issue significance is moderate; chip contract company stakeholder is listed but never developed.

evidence.quote: The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel's company, the chip contract company, the government health department
the issue of maintaining product quality safety while trying to succeed as a business in a competitive field

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Objective arguments for and against shipping are presented with reasonable depth, and conclusions/recommendations follow from them. However, decision-making guidance is directed mainly at Rachel and her company; other stakeholders' decision processes are not separately addressed.

evidence.where: Discussion: To Ship or Not to Ship
evidence.quote: Arguments for Rachel shipping potentially defective servers are as follows.
Rachel should refuse the contract with the government health department.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Structure logically moves from for-arguments to against-arguments to case evidence to conclusion, and the conclusion is well supported. Systematic understanding for ALL stakeholders is not fully achieved (chip company, health department perspectives underdeveloped), so not Excellent.

evidence.quote: the short-term benefit trade-off is greatly outweighed by the potential risks of harm to end-users
the decision to Not Ship is certainly the most ethical path.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Four references including two external case studies (NHS IT failures, VW emissions) with some quantitative evidence (fines, lost letters). However, evidence is one-sided: the pro-shipping arguments (e.g., Apple release strategy) are weakly substantiated, limiting balance.

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: All required sections present; abstract ~140 words; IEEE-style references mostly consistent. But no figures/tables despite permission, several language errors ('DICUSSION', 'ofprofessional', garbled 'have her company might go under'), and reference [3] lacks a URL.

technical_issues.issue: Grammatical errors: 'The economic benefits of could very well...' and 'have her company might go under' are garbled sentences.
Engineers Australia incorrectly abbreviated as 'EACE' (should be EA); code clause numbering quoted inconsistently.
Reference [3] lacks URL; [1] (CNBC iPhone marketing) is tangential to the engineering ethics argument; access dates incomplete.
No figures or tables used despite being permitted; pro-shipping side lacks cited evidence, weakening balance.

overall: A competent, well-structured ethics report that addresses all task requirements, uses relevant case studies and the EA Code of Ethics, and reaches a justified 'not ship' recommendation. Weakened by one-sided evidence, minor language errors, no visual elements, and underdeveloped secondary stakeholders.

feedback.summary: You produced a competent, well-structured ethics report that meets all task requirements, uses the EA Code of Ethics and relevant case studies (NHS, VW), and reaches a justified 'not ship' recommendation. To reach the top band, develop secondary stakeholders more fully, balance your evidence on both sides of the argument, add visual elements, and polish language and referencing details.
next_steps: Add cited evidence supporting the pro-shipping side (e.g., industry data on release-to-market pressures or cost of delays) so both positions are equally substantiated.
Develop the chip contract company and health department as stakeholders: discuss how each should make their decision, not just Rachel and her company.
Include at least one figure or table (e.g., a stakeholder-consequence matrix) and proofread carefully to fix typos and garbled sentences.

criteria.C1: Very good (8/10). You identified several ethical issues (defective shipping, public safety, professional integrity) and clearly enumerated stakeholders with organisational context. To reach Excellent, deepen the significance of each issue and develop the chip contract company stakeholder, which you listed but never discussed.
criteria.C2: Very good (8/10). Your objective for/against arguments have reasonable depth and your recommendation follows from them. For Excellent, extend decision-making guidance to several different stakeholders — currently it is directed mainly at Rachel and her company.
criteria.C3: Very good (8/10). Your structure moves logically from arguments to case evidence to a well-supported conclusion. To reach Excellent, demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for ALL stakeholders — the chip company and health department perspectives remain underdeveloped.
criteria.C4: Very good (8/10). Four references including two external case studies with some quantitative evidence (fines, lost letters) show good research. For Excellent, add both qualitative and quantitative evidence on the pro-shipping side — currently your evidence is one-sided, limiting balance.
criteria.C5: Good (6/10). All required sections are present and references are mostly consistent IEEE style. To improve, use figures or tables (permitted but absent), fix language errors ('DICUSSION', 'ofprofessional', garbled sentences), complete reference [3]'s URL and access dates, and reconsider the tangential CNBC reference.
